degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Amide-bond cleavage produces shorter chains and, under deliberate hydrolysis, material-specific monomers. The cited experiments distinguish caprolactam-rich PA6 products from diamine/diacid recovery for PA66 and PA1010 and amino-acid recovery for PA11 and PA12.

Timescales: The tested polyamides respond differently to hot acid and hydrothermal treatment. Their reactor residence times are not interchangeable and do not define a family lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical reprocessing and dissolution/reprecipitation retain polymer, whereas chemical routes recover monomers. The open room-temperature dissolution study demonstrates PA6/PA66 waste recovery with formic-acid/cosolvent mixtures. Its scope does not establish compatibility with every aliphatic or aromatic polyamide.

Degradation products and pathways: In the cited subcritical-water experiment, PA6 gives a caprolactam-rich liquid through amide cleavage and cyclization. That product mixture describes reactor treatment, not a measured outdoor-weathering leachate.

Timescales: The screening used 350 °C and a 20 min residence time in water, with parallel KOH-assisted trials. Product conversion and recovery at those conditions are distinct from biodegradation.

recyclingAndEndOfLife: PA6 can be reclaimed as polymer by dissolution and precipitation; the cited study uses formic-acid/cosolvent mixtures and remanufactures recovered material. Depolymerization provides a separate caprolactam-recovery route, with purification needed before reuse.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Deliberate carbonate hydrogenation produces bisphenol A and methanol. These are products of the hydrogen/catalyst treatment and should not be treated as a complete inventory of ambient-weathering products.

Timescales: An iron-pincer experiment on approximately 3 mm pellets used THF, 45 bar H2 and 120 °C for 24 h; catalyst loading affected bisphenol-A yield.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical reuse and remolding retain the polymer when quality permits. The cited primary study demonstrates chemical recovery from PC and selected end-of-life articles by iron-catalyzed hydrogenation; it does not establish commercial operation of that process.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Hot pressing atactic PPC can form cyclic propylene carbonate by cyclodepolymerization. A separate iron-catalyzed hydrogenation converts PPC to 1,2-propanediol and methanol; the product set depends on the treatment.

Timescales: Solvent-cast neat PPC films lost 10.7% mass after 24 months in sandy soil at 22 ± 2 °C. In PBS at 37 °C, the same study reports 14.5% mass loss after 12 months.

Environmental persistence: Substantial material remained in these tests. They measure mass loss, not complete carbon mineralization; formulation, molar mass, geometry and environment limit transfer to other PPC articles.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Iron-catalyzed hydrogenation demonstrates recovery of diol feedstock. Thermal conversion to cyclic carbonate is a different recovery target and does not by itself demonstrate a closed polymer-to-polymer loop. These cited experiments do not establish routine post-consumer collection.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The NIST study directly measures yellowing and gloss change in an unpigmented PC–siloxane material containing approximately 20 mass% PDMS. It does not identify a complete molecular degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: The 3.2 mm specimens were exposed to controlled UV at 35, 55 and 70 °C with irradiance and humidity varied. Results are exposure-dependent optical aging, not a single destruction time.

Environmental persistence: The study provides no mineralization or field-disappearance measurement. Its accelerated color/gloss response should not be converted to a litter lifetime.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The NIST study directly measures yellowing and gloss change in an unpigmented PC copolymer containing approximately 15 mass% bisphenol-A ester of a long-chain aliphatic diacid. It does not identify a complete molecular degradation-product inventory.

Timescales: The 3.2 mm specimens were exposed to controlled UV at 35, 55 and 70 °C with irradiance and humidity varied. Results are exposure-dependent optical aging, not a single destruction time.

Environmental persistence: The study provides no mineralization or field-disappearance measurement. Its accelerated color/gloss response should not be converted to a litter lifetime.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patent demonstrates mechanical reuse of defined multilayer film scrap containing a resorcinol arylate/bisphenol-A polyester–carbonate outer layer and a PC/PCTG base. Regrind is repelletized and returned to the base layer beneath a virgin outer layer, with rheological and mechanical properties examined. The result is specific to that film architecture and composition; it does not establish recycling of every polyester–carbonate or routine municipal acceptance.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Formaldehyde is the characteristic decomposition product documented for POM. The copolymer guide distinguishes stabilization by comonomer interruptions from homopolymer behavior.

Timescales: Temperature, contamination and residence time govern processing decomposition. The cited guides do not provide an environmental half-life.

Environmental persistence: Processing instability does not establish rapid degradation in soil or water; no environmental mineralization timescale is reported in these guides.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The manufacturer guides describe clean scrap regrinding and blending with virgin material. Repeated heat history, stabilization, contamination and feed consistency constrain recovery; these instructions concern controlled manufacturing streams.

Degradation products and pathways: The Delrin homopolymer guide identifies formaldehyde as the principal gaseous decomposition product during overheating; emissions can also occur during normal processing.

Timescales: The guide treats degradation as a coupled melt-temperature/residence-time problem, not a fixed time independent of processing conditions.

recyclingAndEndOfLife: Regrinding and remolding clean homopolymer scrap are documented in the guide. Regrind composition and prior processing history must be controlled, with resulting mechanical properties checked for the intended article.

Degradation products and pathways: A directly studied family example is PEEK: Cs2CO3-assisted ethanol/water treatment yields phenol and dibenzofuran. Other PAEKs are not assigned the same product distribution.

recyclingAndEndOfLife: The PEEK example demonstrates matrix destruction to release carbon fibers and recover chemical products. Applicability to other ketone/ether sequences needs separate evidence.

Degradation products and pathways: Cs2CO3-assisted ethanol/water decomposition gives phenol and dibenzofuran; this identifies high-temperature treatment products.

Environmental persistence: A separate artificial-seawater study measured absorption, crystallinity and wear changes under hydrostatic pressures up to 40 MPa. Those changes establish material deterioration, not mineralization or disappearance in the ocean.

Degradation products and pathways: The thiolation study cleaves aryl–oxygen bonds of PEI pellets, yielding bisphenol A and a dithiofunctionalized phenylene-bisphthalimide. It does not establish an ambient degradation-product inventory.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In the studied PMDA/ODA film, ethanolamine breaks imide rings and releases 4,4′-oxydianiline; subsequent hydrolysis and ring reconstruction yields a hydroxyethyl-substituted pyromellitic diimide. These are deliberately generated recovery products.

Timescales: The reported film experiment used a 3 h aminolysis stage at 120 °C, followed by a separate hydrolysis stage. It is not a total environmental decay time.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The study demonstrates aminolysis followed by hydrolysis and product isolation, with separate treatment of crosslinked formulations. Results from the PMDA/ODA film cannot define the recovery chemistry of every aromatic, aliphatic or network polyimide.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The family spans distinct product chemistries. A primary hydrogenation study gives bisphenol A from aromatic BPA-PC and 1,2-propanediol from aliphatic PPC, with methanol also formed.

Timescales: Catalyst, hydrogen pressure and temperature govern the laboratory conversions. A single family degradation timescale would conflate materially different polymers.

Environmental persistence: These reactor experiments do not determine ambient persistence. In particular, evidence for aliphatic PPC must not be transferred to BPA-PC or its copolymers.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The cited study demonstrates chemical feedstock recovery for BPA-PC and PPC. Polymer identity and additives determine whether physical reprocessing or selective chemical treatment is appropriate; neither success proves a common collection route for the entire family.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Direct hydroxylation experiments distinguish PSU, PESU and PPSU: recovered arenols depend on the backbone, including bisphenol A, bisphenol S and dihydroxybiphenyl.

Timescales: The studies require deliberate hydroxide or thiol/base treatment in hot solvent. Their durations describe recovery operations, not environmental persistence.

Environmental persistence: The cited chemical-recovery experiments do not measure environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine disappearance time is established here.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Both intact-polymer regrind and laboratory chemical cleavage are documented for named members. The manufacturer guide concerns controlled sulfone-grade streams; chemical studies recover different aromatic products for different backbones.

recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent proposes acid hydrolysis and feedstock purification for PA46. This is claimed scope, not a demonstrated material-specific process or evidence of commercial recycling.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The primary thermal study measures mass loss of PA610 but does not directly identify its volatile products. Acid hydrolysis is separately documented as a recovery pathway.

Timescales: A patent example reports 97% hydrolysis conversion after 24 h for unfilled, recycled 3–5 mm pellets refluxed in hydrochloric acid with a 120 °C oil bath. The thermal study reports 5% mass loss near 417 °C while heating 5–7.5 mg samples in air at 10 °C/min; this is a temperature-ramp endpoint.

Environmental persistence: Neither experiment establishes PA610 mineralization in soil or water.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The patent demonstrates acid treatment of recycled PA610 pellets, targeting diamine/diacid recovery. Conversion is distinct from isolated monomer yield and does not establish industrial deployment.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The Amodel PPA guide documents thermal degradation during excessive melt residence and changes from repeated processing. Chemical hydrolysis is demonstrated for a named PA66/6T copolyamide in a separate patent; the broad family does not have one product distribution.

Timescales: The patent treats the 35/65 PA66/6T composition under acid reflux for 24 h with a 120 °C oil bath. These are recovery conditions, not an environmental timescale.

Environmental persistence: Neither source establishes mineralization or a family-wide environmental lifetime.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical reuse of dry, clean regrind is documented for named Amodel formulations. The guide requires control of contamination, heat history and regrind proportion. Acid hydrolysis is a separate patent-demonstrated route for the specified PA66/6T composition.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Repeated melt processing changes MXD6 chain structure. In a thesis studying pure MXD6 alongside PET and their blends, viscosity changes were interpreted as competition between chain scission and branching/crosslinking. This is a rheological interpretation, not a resolved inventory of released molecules.

Timescales: Pure MXD6 was extruded through three recycling cycles. Separate isothermal rheology followed behavior for 1,200 s at 270 °C in air or nitrogen; these are processing and accelerated thermal tests.

Environmental persistence: These experiments do not measure biodegradation, mineralization or disappearance in soil or water. No ambient lifetime is assigned.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The thesis demonstrates three melt-reprocessing cycles for pure MXD6 at laboratory scale, with structural and rheological changes that constrain reuse. A manufacturer collaboration reports recycling-compatible polypropylene barrier packaging incorporating MXD6 and supported by APR testing. This is compatibility of the specified multilayer packaging with a PP stream, not recovery of pure MXD6 or blanket acceptance of all MXD6-containing articles. An acid-hydrolysis patent also names MXD6, without demonstrating an MXD6 example.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Vacuum pyrolysis produces hydrogen fluoride, low-volatility chain fragments and a darkening residue. The historical experiment detected SiF4 and water partly because released HF attacked the glass apparatus; those are not an intrinsic PVF product pair.

Timescales: The NBS product experiments used 45 min of heating followed by 30 min at the selected pyrolysis temperature. These high-temperature measurements do not establish ambient persistence.

Environmental persistence: No environmental mineralization time is established by the pyrolysis or separation experiments. Dissolving a film preserves material rather than demonstrating destruction of its carbon backbone.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: A patent demonstrates PVF-film separation using acid/amine ionic-liquid mixtures with DMF, followed by recovery on cooling. Its example dissolves PVF in a 1:3 acetic-acid/tributylamine ionic-liquid-to-DMF mixture at 70 °C in 10 min. This is a patent-reported solvent recovery route.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: In inert-atmosphere pyrolysis, identified monomeric fragments include o-cresol, 2,6-xylenol, 2,4-xylenol and 2,4,6-trimethylphenol. Ether-linked and methylene-linked two-ring fragments were also analyzed.

Timescales: The study concerns rapid thermal decomposition and rearrangement at elevated temperature; it does not determine an outdoor lifetime.

Environmental persistence: The thermal products are not a measured environmental leachate inventory, and no soil or aquatic mineralization time is established.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: Mechanical reclamation is documented for modified PPE blends. Asahi Kasei’s XYRON molding guidance, which explicitly includes PPE/PS grades, permits clean, undegraded sprues, runners and molded articles to be ground, dried and remolded, with regrind levels up to 20%. It discourages regrind where surface appearance is critical. These instructions concern controlled scrap from the listed commercial blends; they do not demonstrate separation of neat PPE from mixed waste, monomer recovery or a general post-consumer collection system.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Iron-photocatalyzed cleavage of PPS produces 1,4-dichlorobenzene, with sulfur, sulfur dioxide and sulfate detected in mechanistic work. Chloroacetic acid arises from the 1,2-dichloroethane co-reagent, not solely from PPS.

Timescales: The study follows irradiation-driven breakdown over hours at room temperature. Added catalyst, oxygen, light and chlorinated co-reagent distinguish this from natural weathering.

Environmental persistence: No environmental half-life or mineralization time is established by this deliberately driven process.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The laboratory study converts commercial resins and selected post-consumer PPS composites, including gram-scale demonstrations. It is a chemical-recovery proof of concept; industrial collection and deployment are not established by the paper.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermogravimetry of Kimya PEKK-A filament shows two stages of thermal mass loss and a carbonaceous residue. The experiment does not collect or identify the evolved molecules; its discussion of possible molecular products draws on other work.

Timescales: The stated filament reaches 5% mass loss at 557 °C during a 10 °C/min ramp in dry synthetic air containing 80% nitrogen and 20% oxygen. This temperature-ramp endpoint is not an isothermal service life or an environmental degradation time.

Environmental persistence: Neither this thermal experiment nor composite reprocessing establishes soil, freshwater or marine mineralization. No ambient disappearance time is assigned.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: A conference study mechanically recycles 60 wt% carbon-fiber/PEKK laminate material by shredding and compression molding. Adding shaped laminate cutouts improves the tested bracket geometry. This demonstrates reuse of a specified composite stream, not depolymerization or indefinite retention of fiber length and properties.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: Thermal ageing of PAI enamel on copper wire first involves additional crosslinking, followed by decomposition attributed to amide and then imide groups. The study reports copper migration into the enamel and accelerated degradation; it does not identify individual evolved molecules.

Timescales: The wire study uses cyclic ageing at 260, 270, 280, 290 and 300 °C, with failure determined by a 900 V, 2 s electrical proof test. This endpoint concerns the specified wire insulation, not a universal PAI degradation duration.

Environmental persistence: Electrical failure under severe thermal ageing does not demonstrate environmental mineralization. No soil, freshwater or marine lifetime is established.
recyclingAndEndOfLife: The Torlon guide permits clean sprues and runners to be reground before post-curing; post-cured material cannot be reprocessed by that route. Torlon 4203L tests show increasing melt viscosity and declining elongation with repeated processing. These results concern specified manufacturing scrap and do not establish recycling of all cured PAI articles.

degradationAndStability:
Degradation products and pathways: The SAMPE study compares thermal decomposition of neat PA6/66 copolyamide with flame-retarded and nanofilled formulations. It measures mass loss and residual char; individual evolved molecules are not identified.

Timescales: The TGA protocol uses approximately 17–18 mg samples heated in nitrogen at 20 °C/min. Its thermal thresholds cannot be converted into a soil or water lifetime.

Environmental persistence: No environmental mineralization or disappearance time is established in the thermal or film-recycling sources.
